events.text: In the temple below the peak the monks have repainted the mountain spirit's shrine behind the main hall. The old man is in it, with his fan and his peach and his tiger. And in the corner of the painting, half hidden by a cloud, there are two eyes nobody remembers asking the painter for.
events.arc: The Old Man of the Mountain

choices.text: Go and look at it at night

effects.log: The painted old man looks very pleased with himself. So, you notice, does the painted tiger.

choices.text: Keep the mountain as he asked: leave the ginseng, let the snow lie

effects.log: For years no root on your mountain is dug before its time. The diggers who come say the mountain hides them now. It does.

events.text: Sickness in the valley: fever, then spots, then the death wail from one house after another. Families who can are fleeing up into your forest with the sick on their backs, to camp by your water, because the old stories say the guest that brings the spots will not follow where you live.

choices.text: Let them camp. Guard the camp at night

effects.log: All summer there are fires by your water. Some of the sick die anyway. More live. When the families go home, they leave the camp stones in a circle, and you never let the forest grow over it.

choices.text: Keep away from the sick

effects.log: You go up into the high rocks until the fires by your water go out. Some of you is ashamed. Some of you is alive.

choices.text: Drive them back down. The sickness will follow them

effects.log: They go back down to the dying valley, carrying their sick. The old story about you changes that year. It is not a kind story any more.

events.text: In the valley there is a family that calls itself after your water. Their great-grandmother was a child carried up to your forest in the sick year, and lived. Every year on the day they came home, they come back up, and light a fire in the circle of stones, and eat rice there, and go down.

choices.text: Sit at the edge of the firelight

effects.log: The youngest children see you and are not afraid. They have been told about you since before they could walk. The fire burns very late that year.

choices.text: Leave them a fish by the fire, unseen

effects.log: They find it in the morning and laugh and cook it. "It still remembers," says the eldest. You do.

events.text: Twenty bandits have made their camp in your valley, in the hollow where the deer drink, because nobody from the villages will come near it any more. They are here because of you. They are robbing the salt road, and the villages blame the valley, which means they blame you.
events.arc: The Hollow Where the Deer Drank

choices.text: Make the valley impossible to sleep in

ok.log: Sounds in the night. Eyes beyond the firelight. Their ox carts found at dawn, gently placed in the river. In a month the bandits move on, and the salt road breathes again.

fail.log: They are bandits, not villagers. They have spears and torches and nothing to lose. You drive them out in the end, but it takes a fight, and you lose a lot of blood doing it.

choices.text: Fall on the camp at midnight

ok.log: The camp is empty by dawn. The captured merchant is still tied to a tree, unhurt, and has a story to tell for the rest of a long life.

fail.log: Twenty spears in the dark.
fail.deathCause: bandit spears, in your own valley

choices.text: Let the humans clear their own road

effects.log: Soldiers come in the autumn and clear the bandits out, and burn the hollow where the deer drank, to be sure. You did not need to do anything. You wish you had.

events.text: A wandering folk painter has been selling pictures of you in the market. They are full of colour, very cheerful and completely wrong. In the painting you are spotted, have the face of a smiling grandmother, and are holding a magpie. People are hanging them over their doors for luck.

choices.text: Let the pictures be. They are bringing people luck

effects.log: For a hundred years the smiling spotted grandmother hangs over doors all over the province. It is the best-loved picture of you there will ever be, and it is not you at all.

choices.text: Show yourself to the painter, so the next one is truer

ok.log: The painter sees you by the river at dusk and goes very quiet. The next pictures are dark, and huge, and true. Nobody buys them. The painter does not care.

fail.log: The painter sees something in the river at dusk, decides it was a log, and paints a smiling grandmother holding a log.

events.text: The whole village is planting rice together in a long line, the farmers' band thumping out the rhythm on drums and gongs, a tall flag at the edge of the paddy. The work song has a new verse this year. It is about you: the thing in the hills that keeps the floods off. They sing it to keep the line moving.

choices.text: Lie on the slope above the paddy where they can see your shadow

effects.log: The line stops singing and then sings louder. They plant the whole valley in a day, a record. The verse stays in the song for two hundred years.

choices.text: Listen from the forest, unseen

effects.log: It is a good song. It is badly in tune. You will hum it to yourself for a very long time.

choices.text: Keep the flood promise: watch the river all summer

effects.log: The summer rain comes and the river rises and does not quite reach the paddies. Nobody knows why. The song knows.

events.text: The new fisher on the lake is young and poor and has made the mistake of casting a net over the deepest water, which is where you sleep. You wake inside it. The fisher is hauling with all their strength and the little boat is tipping toward you.

choices.text: Lie still and let yourself be hauled up to the side

effects.log: Your eyes come up out of the water a hand from the fisher's face. The fisher lets go of the net, very gently, and sits down in the bottom of the boat, and says "excuse me". You find this so polite that you leave the net untorn.

choices.text: Tear the net and sink

effects.log: The fisher hauls up half a net and an empty lake. A poor family loses its net. You feel bad about it all week.

choices.text: Fill the net with fish instead, and slip out

ok.log: The net comes up so full the boat nearly sinks. The fisher rows home singing. From then on, every first catch of the year is thrown back into the deep water.

fail.log: The fish escape with you. The fisher hauls up an empty net and a lot of confused weed.

events.text: On the mountain path at night there is a ghost with no face: smooth as an egg, white as an egg. The old stories say anyone who looks it in the face dies. A traveller with a lantern has just come round the bend and is about to look up.

choices.text: Step out between them

ok.log: You look at the blank face, and it looks at you, and nothing happens. Perhaps you have a face that is too strange to die. The ghost turns away, puzzled. The traveller runs all the way home and lives to be ninety.

fail.log: You look into a face that is not there.
fail.deathCause: the egg-faced ghost on the mountain path

choices.text: Shake the mugwort hanging in the trees, loudly

effects.log: The smell of mugwort rolls down the path. The ghost thins and goes. The traveller never looks up at all, only hurries on, and never knows.

choices.text: Close your own eyes and wait for morning

effects.log: You hear the lantern drop. You hear running. You do not hear anything else. In the morning there is only a broken lantern on the path.

events.text: Below the temple a young scholar on the way to the examinations has drawn a bow on a great black snake that is swallowing a pheasant's chicks. The old monks tell a story about this: a snake that took revenge on a man who shot its mate, and a pheasant that rang the temple bell with its own head to save him. Stories, you have found, like to happen again.

choices.text: Frighten the snake off before the arrow flies

effects.log: The snake drops the nest and goes, alive. Nobody is shot, nobody wants revenge, nobody has to ring a bell with their head. Some stories are best left unrepeated.

choices.text: Let the scholar shoot

effects.log: The arrow flies. That night you lie under the temple and wait, and toward dawn, through the dark, you hear the bell ring once, very softly.

choices.text: Eat the snake

effects.log: Nobody in this story was expecting that, least of all the snake. The pheasant looks at you for a long time and then goes back to its nest.

events.text: An envoy has come from the capital with soldiers and an iron cage. The king, it seems, is building a garden of marvels, and a clerk read a report about your valley. The envoy has ordered the villages to drive the beast into the cage, or pay the grain tax twice.

choices.text: Go into hiding. The villages will pay

effects.log: The villages pay. It is a hungry winter. Nobody says it is your fault. Nobody leaves rice at your spring that year, either.

choices.text: Let them drive you, and break the cage

ok.log: You walk into the cage, and the villages cheer, and the envoy smiles. Then you push. The iron bars bend out like reeds. The envoy writes to the capital that the marvel was unsuitable for the royal garden.

fail.log: The cage is stronger than it looks. It takes you a day and a night to break out, bleeding, and the soldiers chase you for a week.

choices.text: Lead the soldiers away from the villages for a whole season

effects.log: You let them see you, always one ridge away. They follow you over half the province. The villages are left alone. The envoy goes back to the capital thin, sunburnt and empty-handed.

events.text: The king who wanted a garden of marvels is dead. His garden is overgrown. And in the villages of your valley the children play a game called Envoy and Beast, in which the beast always wins, and the child playing the envoy has to sit in a ring of sticks and sulk.

choices.text: Watch the game from the ridge

effects.log: One of them sees you and shouts, and every child in the game bows to the ridge. The envoy sulks harder.

choices.text: Think about the iron bars, and the bent ones

effects.log: Kings die. Cages rust. Children's games last longer than either. You find that comforting.

events.text: Three bad years. The elders have decided the spirit of the pool is angry. Tonight they have left a girl on the flat rock at the water's edge, in white, tied with straw rope, and gone back up the bank with their torches. {npc} is twelve, and not crying, and that is the worst of it.
events.arc: The Girl on the Flat Rock

choices.text: Untie {him} and carry {him} home, through the middle of the village

mem.note: carried me home through the village

effects.log: You walk into the village at midnight with the child on your back. Everyone wakes. Nobody says a word. Nobody is ever offered to your pool again, and every elder who tied that rope dies a little more ashamed than they lived.

choices.text: Bite the rope through and push {him} toward the forest

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for one long moment and then runs, not toward the village, but away from it. You hope it is the right way.

choices.text: Show the elders their mistake: drown the torches

effects.log: Every torch on the bank goes out at once in a great splash. The elders run. In the morning the child walks home alone, wet and furious, and the village is afraid of {npc} for the rest of {his} life.

events.text: {npc} is the village headwoman now, grey-haired and feared and fair. The first thing {he} did in office was to throw the flat rock at the water's edge into the pool. Tonight {he} comes down alone with a lantern and sits where the rock used to be.
events.arc: The Girl on the Flat Rock

choices.text: Rise and sit with {him}

mem.note: sat with me where the rock used to be

effects.log: Neither of you can speak to the other. It does not matter. The lantern burns out, and {npc} sits on in the dark until dawn, and goes home.

choices.text: Stay deep, and let {him} have the place alone

effects.log: Some things a person needs to sit with alone. You keep the water still all night, so the lantern does not flicker.

events.text: A roe deer bursts out of the trees, hunters behind it, and stops at your pool, panting, and looks at you the way creatures sometimes do in the old stories, as if it expected you. A woodcutter with a load of firewood is on the path too, staring at both of you.

choices.text: Hide the deer in your shadow

effects.log: The hunters run past the pool without seeing it. The woodcutter, who saw everything, says nothing. That night the deer comes back and stands on the bank for a long time, and then goes up the mountain toward a place where the old stories say heavenly maidens bathe.

choices.text: Let the woodcutter decide

effects.log: The woodcutter stacks firewood in front of the deer and sits on it, whistling, until the hunters have gone. You suspect there will be a story about this. There usually is.

choices.text: Stay out of it

effects.log: The deer runs on. The hunters run on. The woodcutter looks at you, and you look at the woodcutter, and both of you go home.

events.text: Tomb robbers are digging into the old king's mound on your hill: five of them, lanterns hooded, in the middle of the night. The king has been dead a thousand years. The stone officials at the mound have kept watch the whole time. Tonight, it seems, they need help.

choices.text: Stand behind the stone officials and open your eyes

effects.log: Five lanterns go out at once. Five robbers go down the hill in five directions. One of them leaves a shovel behind that the village uses for years.

choices.text: Fill the hole with earth again before dawn

effects.log: The robbers come back the next night and find the mound whole and grassed, as if no one had touched it. They do not come back the third night.

choices.text: Let them take the gold. The dead do not need crowns

effects.log: The gold crown turns up in a market in the next province, and then in a nobleman's house, and then nowhere. The old king, wherever he is, does not seem to mind.

events.text: A child from the village is lost in the forest in the first snow, and night is falling, and {npc} has sat down under a pine, which is what lost children do, and is going to sleep, which is what lost children must not do.

choices.text: Lie down around the child and keep {him} warm until the torches come

mem.note: kept me warm in the snow when I was lost

effects.log: The search party finds {npc} at dawn, asleep and warm, in a hollow in the snow far too big for a child. Nobody can explain it. {npc} can, and does, for the rest of {his} life.

choices.text: Make a noise to bring the searchers

ok.log: The torches turn toward the sound. They find {npc} cold and frightened and alive.

fail.log: The searchers hear you and turn back, afraid of what made the noise. You stay with {npc} until morning after all, and carry the child to the village edge yourself.

events.text: {npc} has never been afraid of the forest. Now {he} is a woodcutter, and the only one in the village who goes up in the first snow, and the only one who comes home every time. Today {he} leaves a bundle of dried persimmons under the same pine, and sits there for a while, in case.

choices.text: Come and lie in the snow beside {him}

effects.log: {npc} leans back against you as if it were the most natural thing in the world, and eats a persimmon, and gives you one. Snow falls on both of you. It is a good afternoon.

choices.text: Eat the persimmons after {he} has gone

effects.log: {npc} comes back the next day and finds the bundle empty and laughs out loud, alone in the forest, the way people do when something they believed turns out to be true.

events.text: In the market a trader is selling pieces of you: flakes of black lacquer, a yellowed bone, a dried root that is supposedly your heart, each at a terrible price, with a painted banner of a beast that looks nothing like you. People are buying them. One of them is buying a flake for a sick child.

choices.text: Visit the trader's stall at night and leave a real sign

effects.log: In the morning the stall is flattened, the banner is in the river and the ground round the stall is scored by something that was not a man. The trader leaves the province and, in a new province, starts selling something else.

choices.text: Let it be. Humans comfort themselves

effects.log: The child with the flake gets better, the way children often do. The parents put the flake in a little silk bag and keep it for three generations. It is a chip of lacquer.

choices.text: Leave food at the sick child's door instead

effects.log: The child eats well that week. The flake goes in the silk bag anyway, but the family tells the story about the gift.

events.text: A young martial artist has been practising at your waterfall every dawn for a year, trying to cut the falling water so that it stays cut. {npc} cannot do it. You have watched every attempt. Today, frustrated, {he} turns to the plunge pool and shouts, "If there is a spirit here, show me what I am doing wrong!"

choices.text: Rise up through the falling water and let it part around you

mem.note: showed me how the water parts

effects.log: The water does not fight you. It goes round. {npc} stares for a long time, then sheathes the sword and sits down to think. The next year {he} goes down the mountain, and the murim hears about a sword that does not fight the water.

choices.text: Splash {him} off the rock

effects.log: {npc} comes up spluttering, then laughing. "Fair," {he} says. "I asked." {He} practises somewhere drier after that.

choices.text: Stay hidden. Some lessons are only learned alone

effects.log: Three more years. Then one dawn the water stays cut for one heartbeat, and {npc} shouts so loud that you surface in alarm, and the two of you look at each other for the first time.

events.text: Exploring under the mountain, you follow an underground river into a cave nobody has entered for a thousand years. On the wall, in red earth, someone painted hunters with spears, and a great beast, and the beast is winning. Under the painting lies a broken bronze mirror and the bones of whoever painted it.

choices.text: Lie in front of the painting a long time

effects.log: Something like you lived here once and was known. You are not the first. You find that you are glad.

choices.text: Carry the bronze mirror out to the light

effects.log: In the sunlight the broken mirror throws your eyes back at you, cracked and old. A hunter finds it on the riverbank years later, and it ends up in a temple, and the monks say it shows a beast to anyone who looks in it at dusk.

choices.text: Seal the cave again with a rockfall

effects.log: Some places are graves. You leave this one to the painter.

events.text: You explore the ruins of a fortress town on a hill: walls fallen, a stone stupa cracked in two, foundation stones in the grass where houses were. Within your own memory there was a market here, and children, and a well you drank from at night.

choices.text: Find the old well and drink from it again

effects.log: It is choked with leaves, but the water underneath is the same. The town is gone. The water is the same. You lie there until dark, thinking about that.

choices.text: Dig among the stones

ok.log: A child's clay whistle, unbroken. You blow through it, carefully. A crow answers. You keep it for a very long time.

fail.log: A wall you lean on decides it has stood long enough. You get out from under it bruised and dusty, and the crows laugh.

choices.text: Leave. Ruins are only sad if you remember them

effects.log: You do remember them. That is the price of living long. You go down the hill, and it is a good price, and you will pay it again and again.

events.text: Exploring a snowbound valley, you find a hidden hot spring in a hollow of red pines, steaming in the cold. Deer stand at the edge to warm their legs; a pair of cranes are dancing in the steam. Nothing here has ever seen a human, or you.

choices.text: Slide into the hot water and soak

effects.log: Every ache of every winter of your life comes out of you at once. The deer, after a while, come back. The cranes never stopped dancing.

choices.text: Watch the cranes, and learn how they move

effects.log: Step, bow, leap, turn. There is something in it about qi that no human manual has written down. You remember it.

choices.text: Remember the way, and tell no one

effects.log: There is no one to tell. But you remember it, and you come back every hard winter, and it is always there.
